core_obligations: Note that no universal property for the localisation of a module has been established yet, so the isomorphism has to be written down explicitly (proof lines 1525-1527).
Define both maps on fractions: one sending (x/s')/s to x/ss', and the other sending x/t to (x/s')/s for a decomposition t = ss' with s in S and s' in S' (proof lines 1530-1535).
Check well-definedness with respect to the choice of the fraction and verify that the two maps are inverse to each other, which the author marks as easy and straightforward (proof lines 1536-1540).
proof_roadmap: Record that no universal property is available and the isomorphism must be constructed (proof lines 1524-1527).
Write the two mutually inverse maps on fractions and verify they are well defined (proof lines 1528-1541).
difficulty_reason: The proposition states that for multiplicative subsets S and S' of a ring A and an A-module M, the iterated localisation of M at S after S' is isomorphic to the localisation at the product subset (statement lines 1518-1522). The proof does not cite a universal property: the author explicitly notes that none has been proved for module localisation at this point, and therefore writes the isomorphism down on fractions, giving both directions and their decomposition of a denominator as a product, then noting that well-definedness and the inverse property are easy checks (proof lines 1524-1541). Constructing the two maps on elements, rather than deducing the result from a universal property, is the substance; the author's sentence about the omitted routine checks is kept verbatim inside the span. H2.
